title: A Late Passover for Everyone
overview: King Hezekiah revives the long neglected Passover and invites people from both his own southern kingdom and the battered northern kingdom to celebrate it together in Jerusalem.

parts.label: A Passover moved later (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Passover, the yearly meal remembering Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt, could not be held on time because too few priests were ready and the people had not gathered, so the leaders moved it a month later. The chapter does not say why this was allowed, but it likely draws on a rule in the law of Moses that let people who missed Passover keep it one month later.

parts.label: A letter to the north (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: The northern tribes had broken away as a separate kingdom long before, and Assyria had already invaded and carried off many of their people. Hezekiah urges the survivors to come back to God, promising that God is kind and will not turn away from those who return.

parts.label: Mocked, yet some came (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Most northern towns laughed at the king's messengers, but some people from several northern tribes humbled themselves and came anyway. In Judah, the writer says God gave the people a shared will to go.

parts.label: Clearing out old altars (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: The crowd threw out the altars to other gods that had been set up around Jerusalem, dumping them in the Kidron Valley east of the city. Many visitors had not gone through the required cleansing rites, so the Levites, the temple helpers, killed the lambs on their behalf.

parts.label: A prayer for the unprepared (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: Many northerners ate the meal without the proper cleansing, which broke the written rules, so Hezekiah asked God to pardon anyone who sincerely sought God even if not ritually clean. The text says God listened and "healed" the people, which most likely means God spared them the sickness or punishment they feared for breaking the rules.

parts.label: Two weeks of joy (vv. 21-27)
parts.note: The celebration went so well that everyone agreed to double the usual seven days, with the king and his officials giving thousands of animals for sacrifices and shared meals. Locals, northerners and foreigners living among them rejoiced together, and the writer calls it the greatest celebration in Jerusalem since the days of King Solomon.

think: When is it right to bend a rule so that more people can take part, and when does bending it lose something that mattered?
